name: The Zerr-Eiche of Trinitatisplatz

location.address: Trinitatisplatz, opposite the main portal of the Trinitatiskirche, Johannstadt, Dresden

access: Free, standing on a public square (Trinitatisplatz) opposite the church
transport: Tram stop Trinitatisplatz, right on the square (news coverage of a nearby tram diversion names conflicting line numbers across sources, so no specific line is stated here)
story:
Dresden got round to protecting this oak in February 2024, some 130 years after the city planted it. It was raised at the municipal nursery on the Tatzberg and set out on Trinitatisplatz in 1895, facing the main portal of the Trinitatiskirche. Fifty years later the air raids of February 1945 came over Johannstadt, and the oak came through them without serious damage. It then came through the winters that followed, when firewood was scarce enough in Dresden that standing trees disappeared into stoves, and this one was left alone.

It is a Turkey oak, a southern European species with deeply cut leaves and acorns sitting in shaggy, mossy cups rather than the smooth ones a German oak wears. The case for designating it called it the strongest of its kind in Dresden and the third strongest in Saxony, on grounds of age, rarity, form and genetic value.

The trunk measures about 3.84 metres round, worked from a recorded stem diameter of 122 centimetres, although the city's own register line says more than four metres. Nobody has reconciled the two figures and neither is worth much fuss.

Twenty metres tall, standing in the open on a public square with a tram stop at its foot, it is about as easy to reach as a protected tree gets.
verify_notes_removed: Official Dresden natural-monument register (Naturdenkmal, city Umweltamt list reproduced in the Wikipedia 'Liste der Naturdenkmale' table, ND row 168/id 145 per the dedicated article) gives: girth '>4m', stem diameter 122cm, height 20m, age '134 (2024)'. Note: 122cm diameter x pi = ~383cm circumference, which matches the dedicated Wikipedia article's own figure of 3.84m circumference almost exactly, not the register table's '>4m' figure; recorded girth_cm uses the diameter-derived 384cm since two of the three figures agree on it, but the register's own '>4m' entry is a minor mismatch worth a reader correction. Planted 1895 after being raised at the city's Tatzberg nursery (per dawo-dresden.de and Radio Dresden coverage of the Feb 2024 designation), which would make it ~131 years old in 2026 versus the register's implied ~136; both given as one broad band. Third-strongest Turkey oak in Saxony and the strongest in Dresden per the designation rationale (history, age, rarity, imposing form, genetic value). Survived the WWII air raids on Dresden without serious damage and was spared the postwar firewood shortage. Newly designated a Naturdenkmal in February 2024, so alive and monitored as of that date.

name: The Plane Tree of Albertplatz

location.address: Albertplatz, on the traffic island toward Bautzner Strasse, Innere Neustadt, Dresden

access: Free, standing on a traffic island in the middle of a public square, accessible at any time
transport: Albertplatz tram and bus interchange, right on the square
story:
This plane tree lives on a traffic island. Albertplatz is one of the busiest interchanges in Dresden, a circle of tram and bus routes in the Neustadt, and the tree stands out in the middle of it toward Bautzner Strasse, twenty-five metres tall with a crown roughly as wide as it is high.

It was planted around 1885, when that ground was open and quiet. Everything else arrived later: the trams, the traffic, the night of 13 February 1945 and the long rebuilding after it, forty years of the GDR, and the Neustadt's more recent turn into the loudest quarter in the city. The tree has stayed put through all of it on its own island, which is the closest thing to a fixed point Albertplatz has. Dresden made it a natural monument on 3 January 1985, by the same council resolution that protected the oak on Fetscherplatz.

A London plane is a hybrid of the American and the Oriental plane, and it was planted across European cities for exactly the qualities on show here. It takes heat, compacted soil and dirty air better than almost anything else with a trunk, and it sheds its bark in pale plates through the summer instead of letting the grime build up.

Its trunk measures 3.30 metres round. Both the register and the city's own record agree on the figure, which is rarer than it sounds.
verify_notes_removed: Register (city Naturdenkmal list, ND 26) and dedicated Wikipedia article agree: height ~25m, crown diameter similar, trunk circumference 3.30m. Planted around 1885 on open ground at Albertplatz. Independently confirmed as ND 26 by Stadtwiki Dresden (a separate, non-Wikipedia community wiki), which lists it by name, number and district. Designated a natural monument by Dresden city council resolution of 3 January 1985, the same resolution that protected the Fetscherplatz oak (dre_003) and the Mozartstrasse ironwood tree (not delivered, see leads: stands in a private front garden). A hybrid between the American and Oriental plane, chosen historically as a hardy, heat-tolerant street tree. No felling or storm-damage reports found in a targeted 2024-2026 news search.

name: The Oak of Fetscherplatz
access: Free, standing on a public square, visible and reachable at all times
transport: Tram stop Fetscherplatz, directly beside the tree
story:
In 1949 an architect built a tram shelter around this tree rather than move either of them. Herbert Schneider put his waiting kiosk on Fetscherplatz so close to the trunk that the roof had to curve to make room for the oak, four years after the air raids, in a city with more urgent things to be careful about. The two have shared the corner ever since.

The tree is an overcup oak, a North American species and an unlikely thing to find holding down a square in Johannstadt. It went in around 1900, when the place was still called Fuerstenplatz, and it has since put out a crown about thirty-two metres across, wider than the tree is tall. That crown is effectively the roof of the square. Twenty-five metres up, 3.35 metres round at the trunk, and the only real shade anyone waiting for a tram is going to get.

Dresden protected it as a natural monument on 3 January 1985, in the same council resolution that covered the plane tree on Albertplatz.

If you are there in autumn, look at the acorns on the ground. The cup on this species swallows almost the entire nut, which is where the name comes from and the quickest way to tell it apart from every other oak in the city.
verify_notes_removed: Register (ND 27) and dedicated Wikipedia article agree: height ~25m, crown diameter ~32m (dominates the whole square), trunk circumference 3.35m. A North American species (Quercus lyrata, native to the US), planted around 1900 when the square was still called Fuerstenplatz. Independently confirmed as ND 27 by Stadtwiki Dresden. Protected since the same 3 January 1985 city council resolution as the Albertplatz plane (dre_002). In 1949 architect Herbert Schneider built a tram-stop waiting kiosk so close to the trunk that its roof curves around the tree, a well documented and photographed detail. Not to be confused with an unrelated, separate 375-year-old oak on Hueblerstrasse in Blasewitz that was felled in mid-2025 after losing a fight with a fungal disease (dawo-dresden.de, June 2025); that tree is a different oak in a different district. No felling or health reports found for this Fetscherplatz specimen.

name: The Splittereiche

location.address: Grosser Garten, on the open lawn roughly 40 metres south of the Mosaikbrunnen (Mosaic Fountain), Dresden

access: Free, standing in the open on a public lawn inside the Grosser Garten park, open during park hours
transport: Enter the Grosser Garten and walk to the Mosaikbrunnen; nearest tram stops are around Strassburger Platz or Lenneplatz, roughly a 10-15 minute walk into the park (approximate, not independently timed)
story:
This oak is named after its wounds. On the nights of 13 and 14 February 1945 the bombing of Dresden reached the Grosser Garten, and splinters tore open one side of the trunk along roughly eight metres of its height. The tree survived. The damage is still there and still obvious, which is how it came to be called the Splittereiche, the splinter oak.

It was already old when that happened. An assessment made in the 2010s put it at between 250 and 300 years, a range nobody has narrowed since and which is itself a decade out of date by now. It stands twenty-seven metres tall with a trunk over six metres round, out on open lawn a short walk south of the Mosaikbrunnen, so you see the whole shape of it from a distance before you get to the scar.

On 8 May 2017, the seventy-second anniversary of the end of the war in Europe, a memorial plaque went up beside it carrying a line from Mark Twain: time may heal all wounds, but it is a lousy cosmetician. The year after, the city fitted metal sheeting over the damaged flank, because visitors picking at the old injury were making it worse.

We have not found it listed individually in Dresden's register of natural monuments. It stands inside a protected historic park instead, and it is the tree people in that park come to find.
verify_notes_removed: A pedunculate oak (Quercus robur), height ~27m, trunk circumference 'over 6 metres', age assessed at 250 to 300 years (assessment dated to the 2010s per de.wikipedia, so now a decade or more further on; kept as the source's own vague range rather than sharpened). Hit by bomb splinters during the RAF/USAAF air raids on Dresden of 13-14 February 1945; survived, with visible one-sided trunk damage extending about 8m up, which is how it got its name (Splittereiche = 'splinter oak'). Protective metal sheeting installed 2018 to stop visitors worsening the wound. A memorial plaque was unveiled on 8 May 2017 (72nd anniversary of VE Day), quoting Mark Twain: 'Time may heal all wounds, but it is a lousy cosmetician.' Sources: dedicated de.wikipedia article, baumkunde.de (independent German tree register), monumentale-eichen.de (specialist oak register), and treedd.de (local Dresden tree-advocacy group), all agreeing on location, species and history; this is well beyond the two-source bar. FLAG: not found in the official city Naturdenkmal list (it may be protected by other means, e.g. as part of the listed Grosser Garten historic park, rather than individually designated), so its formal protection status is unconfirmed even though its identity and history are solid. FLAG: 2025-08 news coverage describes the Grosser Garten felling roughly 300 to 425 drought- and disease-weakened trees park-wide over the 2025/26 season because of climate-stress dieback; no source found naming the Splittereiche specifically among them, but given the park-wide mortality crisis this specimen is worth a fresh health check before the page ships or shortly after.
